name: Captain Ben Hassell
bio:
Captain William Benjamin "Ben" Hassell stands as one of the most legendary maritime figures in the history of the Dutch Caribbean. Born into the rugged volcanic isolation of Saba in the late nineteenth century, Captain Ben Hassell rose to become a master mariner, fleet owner, and mercantile pioneer whose life exemplified the extraordinary seafaring tradition of his home island [1]. Operating during a transformative era in Caribbean history—when wooden sailing schooners were the primary conduit for communication, commerce, and human mobility—Hassell built a maritime network that spanned from the Eastern Caribbean to the bustling docks of New York City [2]. His career not only sustained the local economy of Saba through decades of global upheaval but also established an enduring legacy of navigational excellence that continues to define the island's cultural identity today.

### Early Life and the Saban Seafaring Tradition

To understand the trajectory of Captain Ben Hassell's extraordinary life, one must first understand the unique geographical and social reality of Saba at the turn of the twentieth century. Known as the "Unspoiled Queen" of the Caribbean, Saba is a five-square-mile volcanic peak jutting dramatically out of the Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea [1]. Unlike neighboring islands blessed with sweeping sandy bays and protected natural harbors, Saba possesses steep rocky cliffs and treacherous shoreline surf. For generations, every pound of cargo, every letter, and every traveler had to be brought ashore through challenging swells at Fort Bay or ladder-like cliff paths [3].

![Scenic view over Windwardside and Mount Scenery on Saba, illustrating the rugged volcanic landscape from which Captain Ben Hassell set sail.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/View_over_Windwardside_and_Mt_Scenery,_Saba.jpg)

In this unforgiving environment, agriculture alone could not sustain the island's growing population. Consequently, Saban men turned to the sea with a single-minded devotion that quickly earned them renown across the Western Hemisphere [2]. Young boys routinely left school before their teenage years to serve as cabin boys on inter-island sloops and ocean-going schooners. William Benjamin Hassell was born directly into this maritime heritage. Growing up among a tight-knit community of sailors and shipbuilders, young Ben absorbed the intricate arts of seamanship, celestial navigation, and maritime meteorology from his elders [1].

From his earliest days aboard local vessels, Hassell exhibited an intuitive understanding of wind patterns and ocean currents. He learned to read the subtle changes in the Caribbean sky—identifying the early warning signs of approaching tropical cyclones and mastering the complex channels between the Leeward Islands [2]. By his early twenties, Hassell had transitioned from a skilled deckhand to a fully qualified ship master, earning the title of Captain and commanding the respect of seasoned sailors twice his age.

### Rise to Prominence and the Schooner Fleet

As Captain Ben Hassell's reputation as a reliable and intrepid navigator grew, so too did his entrepreneurial ambitions. Recognizing that Saba's economic survival depended entirely on robust trade links with the outside world, Hassell began acquiring and operating his own sailing vessels [2]. Over the course of his illustrious career, he would own and operate over twenty fine schooners—a remarkable fleet that placed him among the most prominent ship owners in the Eastern Caribbean [1].

> "To be born on Saba in the nineteenth century was to inherit the sea as both a birthright and a battleground. Captain Ben Hassell did not merely navigate the Caribbean; he commanded its currents, transforming wooden schooners into lifelines for an isolated people." [2]

During the early decades of the twentieth century, Hassell's schooners became the vital economic engine of Saba. At the time, the women of Saba were producing exquisite hand-crafted lace, known internationally as "Saban Drawn Thread Work" [4]. Captain Ben Hassell's vessels transported this delicate artisanal lace to lucrative markets in Barbados, St. Kitts, Puerto Rico, and the United States, returning with essential foodstuffs, lumber, building materials, and dry goods [1]. Whenever one of Hassell's schooners dropped anchor off Fort Bay, it was an island-wide event; longboats manned by muscular Saban rowers would brave the surf to offload barrels of flour, sugar, salt, and raw linen cloth that sustained everyday life [3].

![Fort Bay, the historic and only maritime gateway of Saba, where cargo schooners anchored amidst challenging Atlantic swells.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Fort_Bay,_Saba.jpg)

Beyond mere trade, Captain Ben's fleet served as the primary passenger service connecting Sabans to the wider world. Young men seeking employment in the oil refineries of Curaçao and Aruba, or on international merchant marine vessels sailing out of North American ports, relied on Captain Ben's schooners for their passage [2]. His vessels were reputed to be impeccably maintained and run with strict discipline, ensuring safety across hazardous open-water routes.

### The Flagships: Esther Anita and Mona Marie

Among the numerous vessels that comprised Captain Ben Hassell's fleet, two schooners achieved legendary status in Caribbean maritime annals: the *Esther Anita* and the *Mona Marie* [1]. Each vessel represented the pinnacle of wooden shipbuilding and served distinct roles within Hassell's expansive commercial enterprise.

The *Esther Anita* was a magnificent multi-masted schooner celebrated for its speed and cargo capacity [1]. Commanded personally by Captain Ben and his most trusted lieutenants, the *Esther Anita* regularly plied the arduous trade route between the Eastern Caribbean and New York City. Archival photographs and harbor records document the *Esther Anita* docked prominently along the East River near the Brooklyn Bridge, unloading tropical produce, salt, and spices before loading American manufactured goods, hardware, and lumber for the return voyage to the West Indies [2]. Navigating a wooden sailing vessel through the stormy waters of the North Atlantic required exceptional nautical skill, and Captain Ben's successful round-trip voyages established his reputation in international maritime circles.

The *Mona Marie*, another flagship of the Hassell line, became equally famous, particularly for the familial legacy it fostered [2]. In a testament to the exceptional seafaring training instilled within the Hassell family, Captain Ben entrusted the command of the *Mona Marie* to his son, Captain Laurie Hassell, when Laurie was just nineteen years old [1]. Under young Laurie's command, the *Mona Marie* conducted extensive inter-island commerce, transporting everything from agricultural produce to drums of gasoline across the Lesser Antilles. Tragically, the *Mona Marie* met its end during the turbulent years of World War II when it was intercepted and torpedoed by a German U-boat off the coast of St. Vincent—a grim reminder of the immense perils faced by Caribbean merchant mariners during global conflicts [2].

### Navigation, Wartime Perils, and Maritime Commerce

Captain Ben Hassell operated in an era defined by profound technological transitions and international turmoil. During the First and Second World Wars, Caribbean maritime trade was severely disrupted by German naval operations and submarine warfare [2]. While steamships and early motorized freighters began displacing traditional sailing vessels in major global ports, inter-island commerce in the West Indies remained heavily dependent on agile wooden schooners that could navigate shallow island reefs and operate without imported bunker fuel [4].

In this challenging environment, Captain Ben Hassell collaborated and competed with a distinguished cadre of regional master mariners. He was a central figure in the esteemed Saban "schooner-owning fraternity," operating alongside legendary contemporaries such as [Ernest Alfred Johnson](/profiles/ernest-alfred-johnson), [Thomas Charles Vanterpool](/profiles/thomas-charles-vanterpool), and [Thomas Simmons](/profiles/thomas-simmons) [3]. Together, these captains formed an informal commercial network that stabilized the regional supply chain during times of economic depression and maritime blockade.

> "In an era before modern radar and engine-driven cargo fleets, the Saban schooner masters were the undisputed sovereigns of the Eastern Caribbean trade. Captain Ben Hassell stood at the pinnacle of that fraternity—a mariner whose vessels carried the hopes, labor, and sustenance of an entire island." [3]

The economic impact of Hassell's shipping activities extended far beyond Saba. His schooners were regular visitors to Bridgetown in Barbados and Basseterre in St. Kitts, where regional political and labor leaders, including future statesman [Robert Llewellyn Bradshaw](/profiles/robert-llewellyn-bradshaw), recognized the indispensable role of inter-island shipping in fostering working-class solidarity and regional integration [2]. By maintaining regular communication and trade between British, Dutch, and French colonial territories, Captain Ben Hassell inadvertently helped forge a shared Caribbean identity rooted in mutual interdependence.

### Family Legacy and Enduring Impact on Saba

In his later years, Captain Ben Hassell established a residence in Barbados with his beloved wife, Mary Love, where they raised eight children [1]. Even while residing in Bridgetown—a major shipping hub of the British West Indies—Hassell maintained his deep emotional and commercial ties to Saba. His home became a welcoming sanctuary for itinerant Saban sailors making port in Barbados, providing them with news from home, employment opportunities aboard his vessels, and guidance in navigating their maritime careers [2].

Captain Ben's influence as a mentor shaped an entire generation of master mariners. Numerous distinguished Saban ship captains, including Peter Every and Diederick Ambrose Every, began their maritime lives as humble cabin boys aboard Captain Ben's schooners [1]. Under his rigorous tutelage, these young men mastered the discipline, mathematical precision, and courage required to command ocean-going vessels, ensuring that Saba's seafaring reputation endured long after sail gave way to diesel power.

Furthermore, Captain Ben Hassell's lineage continued to profoundly impact Caribbean business and society. Through his descendants, his entrepreneurial spirit flourished; he was the grandfather of the Goddard family, who went on to establish Goddard Enterprises, one of the most successful multinational conglomerates in the Caribbean with extensive operations spanning retail, aviation catering, and maritime services across Barbados, St. Kitts, and beyond [1].

Today, the memory of Captain William Benjamin "Ben" Hassell is enshrined in the historical fabric of Saba. In recognition of his monumental contributions to the island's heritage, one of the prestigious "Captains' Suites" at Juliana’s Hotel in Windwardside is dedicated in his honor, celebrating his legacy alongside fellow icons of the sea [3]. Local historians, museum archives, and folk songs continue to recount the exploits of his fleet. Captain Ben Hassell remains an immortal symbol of Saba's golden age of sail—a visionary navigator who harnessed the winds of the Atlantic to secure the dignity, prosperity, and place in history of the Caribbean's Unspoiled Queen [4].
contributions:
Captain William Benjamin "Ben" Hassell played a transformative role in the economic and social development of Saba and the wider Eastern Caribbean during the first half of the twentieth century. As the owner and commander of over twenty commercial sailing schooners—including the celebrated flagships *Esther Anita* and *Mona Marie*—Hassell established critical maritime trade routes connecting Saba with New York City, Barbados, St. Kitts, and Puerto Rico. His shipping network served as the primary lifeline for an isolated volcanic island lacking a natural harbor, enabling the export of Saba's famous hand-crafted lace ("Drawn Thread Work") and agricultural produce while importing vital foodstuffs, lumber, and manufactured goods. During eras of global depression and wartime supply disruptions, his fleet sustained regional commerce and ensured the survival of coastal communities across the Lesser Antilles.

Beyond his mercantile achievements, Captain Hassell made an indelible contribution to maritime education and professional seamanship in the West Indies. He mentored scores of young Saban cabin boys who rose under his rigorous discipline to become celebrated master mariners in their own right, cementing Saba's international reputation as a prolific nursery for world-class navigators. Operating alongside fellow maritime pioneers, his enterprise laid the foundational infrastructure for modern Caribbean inter-island trade. Furthermore, his familial legacy helped spawn major regional enterprises, leaving a lasting imprint on the economic landscape of the Caribbean that endures to this day.
